newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Bras and bulldozers form S.Korean labour folklore.
newsitem.headline: Bras and bulldozers form S.Korean labour folklore.

text.p: In the hot summer of 1976, female workers at the Dong-il Textile Company staged an audacious protest: they stripped off their clothes and confronted startled police wearing only bras and panties.
"We heard they wouldn't touch us if we were naked," recalled Yi Chong-kak, a founder of South Korea's first all-woman union at Dong-il.
The women were in for a surprise.
Riot police charged in and dragged them screaming and kicking into police buses.
Two years later, during elections for the union president, managers hired thugs who tossed buckets of human excrement over the women voters.
Repelled by the stench, the women fled and the vote was cancelled.
"We tightened our belts to suppress hunger, and we worked hard thinking it was patriotic," said Yi, recalling harsh days toiling over spools of thread.
Appeals to patriotism no longer motivate South Korea's workforce. Frustrations built up during forced-pace industrialistion under military rule burst into violence after democracy flowered in 1987.
In that year, 30,000 Hyundai workers in Ulsan drove bulldozers, cranes, and giant metal cutters into the ranks of riot police. Seven million working days were lost in 1987.
Two years later it took an amphibious assault by 10,000 troops to end a 109-day strike at the Hyundai shipyard.
The Dong-il bra-and-panties protest is now part of labour folklore.

And one of the icons of the union movement is a young textile worker who doused himself in petrol and set himself on fire in 1970. "Don't let my death be useless," Chun Tae-il reportedly screamed as flames consumed his body.
Chun's gruesome death was depicted in a feature film released last year. It has sparked copy-cat self-immolations by other fanatics.
In May 1995, Hyundai Motor worker Yang Bong-soo ended his life in flames after being dismissed for halting production of a new car model.
In an eerie echo last week, another Hyundai car worker staggered towards riot police with his clothes blazing. Three colleagues were injured trying to save his life.

Former strongman Park Chung-hee, the architect of South Korea's economic takeoff, branded unionists as communists and used the infamous spy agency then known as the Korean CIA to harrass labour activists.

The Korean CIA was reborn as the Agency for National Security Planning. Its wings were clipped by President Kim Young-sam after he took office in 1993, but a new law passed last month restored its powers.
Kim earned his place in labour history in 1979 when 50 female wig factory workers staged a sit-in at his opposition party headquarters.
The three-day protest ended with a police raid and the death of a female worker.
Kim is now on the other side of the fence after his ruling New Korea Party rammed through parliament a new labour law that has sparked almost three weeks of labour protests.
